strengths: Conceptual Novelty: Formulating adversarial attacks at the concept level rather than as perturbations of a single fixed image provides an interesting and fresh perspective on unrestricted adversarial attacks.

Sound Theoretical Grounding: Building upon the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al., 2024), the paper provides intuitive mathematical justification (Theorems 1 and 2) showing how expanding the variance of the distance distribution reduces divergence to the victim distribution.

High Perceptual Quality and Concept Preservation: The qualitative and quantitative results (user study, CLIP scores, and multiple no-reference IQA metrics) demonstrate that the proposed method avoids typical distortion and artifacts observed in competing methods like DiffAttack.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The authors evaluate across various surrogate architectures (ResNet-50, MobileNet-V2, ViT-Base), target black-box classifiers, and adversarially trained defense models, complemented by sensitivity analyses on candidate pool size $M$.
weaknesses: High Computational Overhead: The method requires fine-tuning an SDXL LoRA (~20 minutes) and then fine-tuning an unconditional diffusion model (~8 hours per concept on an H100 GPU). This significantly restricts the scalability and applicability of the attack compared to standard test-time attack methods.

Loose Transferability Metric: Because targeted transferability across 1,000 ImageNet classes is inherently difficult, the paper relies on Top-100 success rate for transferability. A top-100 criterion is quite permissive (random chance is already 10%), making it harder to gauge true targeted transfer strength.

Simplified Theoretical Assumptions: Theorem 1 assumes 1D Gaussian distributions with identical means between instance- and concept-level distributions. While helpful for basic intuition, this is an oversimplification of high-dimensional multimodal image manifolds.

Dependence on Sample Selection: The attack heavily relies on sampling $M$ candidates (e.g., $M=10$) from $p_{\mathrm{adv}}$ and filtering based on classifier confidence. While standard in probabilistic attack setups, this multi-sample filtering contributes noticeably to the reported attack success rates.

strengths: Principled probabilistic framework: Generalizing single-instance unrestricted adversarial attacks to concept-based attacks provides a novel perspective on how semantic coverage and variance impact attack success.

Theoretical justification: Theorems 1 and 2 offer clear mathematical intuition demonstrating how expanding the variance of the distance distribution reduces the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the victim distribution.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates white-box and transfer attacks across multiple victim architectures (CNNs, ViTs, and adversarially robust models), complemented by extensive no-reference image quality assessments and a human user study.

High visual fidelity: Qualitative and quantitative results show that the proposed approach retains natural appearance and high fidelity to the underlying concept compared to existing latent-space unrestricted attack baselines.
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead: Fitting a dedicated LoRA and subsequently training an unconditional diffusion model for ~8 hours on an H100 GPU per concept significantly hampers the practical feasibility and deployability of the attack.

Loose transferability metric: For black-box transferability, success is reported solely under the Top-100 criterion on ImageNet-1k, which is relatively permissive (a random classifier has a 10% base rate), while exact Top-1 and Top-5 transfer rates are omitted.

Simplifying theoretical assumptions: Theorem 1 relies on strong assumptions, namely that the distance distribution is Gaussian with identical mean and isotropic variance, which deviates substantially from the complex, high-dimensional manifolds modeled by diffusion models.

Limited dataset scale: Experiments are restricted to 26 concepts from DreamBooth and 30 target classes, resulting in a somewhat constrained scope compared to standard large-scale adversarial evaluation benchmarks.

strengths: Novel Conceptual Framing: Formulating unrestricted adversarial attacks at the concept level rather than the single-instance level is an intriguing direction that naturally connects generative modeling and adversarial machine learning.

Comprehensive Perceptual Evaluation: The paper evaluates generated images using a wide battery of no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics (MUSIQ, TReS, NIMA, ARNIQA, DBCNN, HyperIQA), CLIP similarity, and a human user study.

Extensive Surrogate Architecture Testing: The appendix provides experiments across multiple distinct surrogate backbones (ResNet-50, MobileNet-V2, ViT-Base) against both standard and adversarially trained victim classifiers.
weaknesses: Questionable Threat Model and Extreme Computational Infeasibility: The proposed pipeline requires training an SDXL LoRA (~20 minutes), generating augmented data via GPT-4o, and then fine-tuning a pixel-level diffusion model from scratch for 8,000 steps per concept (~8 hours on an NVIDIA H100 GPU) just to attack a single concept. This makes the attack extraordinarily expensive and impractical under realistic threat models, blurring the line between an adversarial attack and computationally intensive generative synthesis.

Very Weak Transferability Evaluation Metric (Top-100): Because top-1 targeted black-box success was near zero across all methods, the authors report Top-100 success rates on ImageNet-1000. On a 1,000-class classifier, predicting the target class within the top 10% is an extremely loose criterion that does not substantiate strong claims of transferable targeted attacks.

Limited Theoretical Depth and Overly Simplistic Assumptions: Theorem 1 is an elementary univariate Gaussian variance exercise that assumes $p_{\text{dis}}(\cdot | x_{\text{ori}})$ and $p_{\text{dis}}(\cdot | \mathcal{C}_{\text{ori}})$ share the identical mean $\mu$ and differ only in variance, which does not reflect the complex, multi-modal, high-dimensional manifolds of natural images. Theorem 2 is an algebraic identity resulting from the cancellation of the partition function in Gibbs distributions, providing minimal theoretical novelty.

Incremental Novelty Over ProbAttack: The core probabilistic formulation, objective relaxation, and Langevin dynamics sampling framework are directly inherited from Zhang et al. (NeurIPS 2024). The main modification is populating the training set with SDXL/DreamBooth samples rather than a single image.

Limited Evaluation Scale: The empirical evaluation is conducted on only 26 concepts from the DreamBooth dataset, which represents a narrow domain of objects/identities and restricts the generalizability of the empirical conclusions.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated conceptual expansion: Extending adversarial attacks from perturbing a single image to generating instances from a concept-level distribution provides a fresh and principled perspective for unrestricted adversarial attacks.

Principled probabilistic formulation: The paper builds cleanly upon the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al., 2024b), framing the problem as expanding the distance distribution overlap with the victim distribution.

Solid empirical results: The proposed method demonstrates strong white-box targeted attack success rates (e.g., >94% across different architectures) and competitive transferability, while maintaining high visual realism and concept fidelity as evidenced by no-reference IQA metrics and user study.

Extensive experimental suite: The evaluation covers multiple surrogate backbones (ResNet, MobileNet-V2, ViT, ConvNeXt, robust models) and provides thorough ablations on sample selection strategies (aggressive vs. conservative) and candidate sizes.
weaknesses: High computational cost and complex pipeline: Generating attacks requires fine-tuning an SDXL LoRA, querying GPT-4o, generating augmented datasets, and subsequently fine-tuning an unconditional diffusion model for ~8 hours on an NVIDIA H100 per concept. This limits practical usability compared to existing unrestricted or diffusion-based attacks.

Incremental theoretical depth: Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 represent relatively direct properties of Gibbs distributions and standard KL divergence expansions under the assumption that the victim normalizing constant cancels out.

Inherently easier task compared to single-image baselines: By allowing the attack to vary pose, viewpoint, and background freely across an entire distribution of scenes, finding an adversarial instance is fundamentally less constrained than traditional or single-image unrestricted attacks (e.g., DiffAttack, ACA, ProbAttack with |Cori|=1), making direct comparisons somewhat advantageous to the proposed method.

Limited dataset scale: Due to the high cost of per-concept fine-tuning, the empirical evaluation is restricted to 26 concepts from DreamBooth, which is modest compared to standard adversarial robustness benchmarks.

strengths: Principled probabilistic formulation: The paper effectively generalizes the probabilistic view of adversarial attacks (Zhang et al., 2024b) from single-image perturbation distributions to broader concept distributions, formalizing the relationship through well-motivated theoretical analyses (Theorems 1 and 2).

High visual fidelity and concept preservation: By leveraging modern generative pipelines (SDXL LoRA augmentation and score-based sampling), the generated unrestricted adversarial samples preserve fine-grained identity details significantly better than existing latent-space manipulation baselines (e.g., DiffAttack, ACA), supported by both quantitative IQA metrics and human user studies.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The experimental evaluation is thorough, benchmarking against competitive baselines across multiple victim architectures (ResNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, MobileNet-V2) and robust/adversarially trained models across white-box and transferability settings.
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead: The pipeline requires fine-tuning an individual diffusion model for each concept (~8 hours on an NVIDIA H100) alongside LoRA concept augmentation (~20 minutes), making it substantially more resource-intensive and less practical than test-time optimization or inversion-based methods.

Blurred distinction between adversarial attacks and generative failure discovery: Because the pipeline synthesizes novel images from a generative model rather than perturbing an existing observed instance, the method borders on discovering natural failure cases or synthetic blind spots of classifiers rather than conventional adversarial example generation.

Limited dataset scale and diversity: The empirical evaluation is constrained to 26 specific concepts from DreamBooth, which primarily comprise centered, isolated physical objects and pets, leaving open questions about performance on complex, cluttered multi-object scenes.

Dependence on candidate sample filtering: The sampling-and-selection stage ($M=10$ candidate generation followed by AGGR/CONS filtering) introduces a notable heuristic component that heavily influences the trade-off between attack success rate and concept fidelity.

strengths: Novel Conceptual Threat Model: The paper thoughtfully shifts the threat modeling of unrestricted adversarial attacks from single-image perturbations to identity/concept-level distributions, allowing variations in viewpoint, pose, and background while maintaining semantic identity.

Principled Probabilistic Grounding: Building upon recent probabilistic formulations of adversarial attacks, the formulation cleanly interprets adversarial generation as sampling from the intersection of a victim distribution and a broadened concept distance distribution.

Comprehensive Evaluation Suite: The paper provides extensive experiments across multiple architectures (CNNs, ViTs, adversarially trained models), including no-reference image quality metrics, CLIP similarity scores, human perceptual evaluation (user study), and sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: Incremental Algorithmic Novelty over Prior Work: The algorithmic framework strongly relies on ProbAttack (Zhang et al., 2024b). Operationally, the core methodological adaptation consists of fine-tuning the underlying diffusion model on an augmented set of ~30 images per concept instead of a single image, followed by rejection/ranking sampling among M candidates.

Extreme Computational Cost and Practical Infeasibility: The proposed pipeline is remarkably heavy for generating attacks: it requires generating synthetic prompts via GPT-4o, training an SDXL LoRA, and then fine-tuning a diffusion model for approximately 8 hours on an NVIDIA H100 GPU per concept. This drastically limits practical applicability compared to standard unrestricted attack baselines.

Limited Theoretical Depth: The theoretical findings are relatively elementary. Theorem 1 essentially relies on the standard derivative of the log-partition function for exponential families/Gibbs distributions, and relies on an idealized unimodal formulation that oversimplifies the complex, multimodal distribution learned by modern diffusion models. Theorem 2 is simply an algebraic cancellation of the victim partition constant.

Narrow Evaluation Scale: The empirical evaluation is constrained to only 26 specific object concepts from the DreamBooth dataset, making it difficult to assess how well the approach generalizes to complex real-world concepts, multiple co-occurring objects, or broader domains.

Modest Black-Box Transferability: Despite the claims of improved efficiency, actual black-box targeted transferability remains low across standard models (top-1 transfer rates are near 1%, and even top-5 rates remain mostly in single digits), indicating limited utility in realistic black-box attack settings.
